Entries.Title: From a changed file to an uploaded version
Entries.Purpose: Your working files, staged contents, local commits, and uploaded commits describe four different states. Save files in your editor before inspecting them in GitCompass.
Entries.Prerequisites: A disposable practice project, an installed Git executable, and a deliberate access choice.
Entries.Effects: Staging changes the index. Commit records the reviewed index locally. Push publishes recorded commits to an explicit destination. Unsaved editor buffers and unstaged contents are not included.
Entries.WhenToPause: Pause if unexpected files are staged, the current branch is wrong for a configured task, remote knowledge is stale, or an interrupted operation exists.
Entries.Example:
git status
git diff --no-ext-diff --no-textconv
git add -- practice.txt
git diff --cached --no-ext-diff --no-textconv
git commit -m 'Explain the first practice change'
git push <reviewed-remote> HEAD:<reviewed-branch>
Entries.Outcome: A commit can exist safely on this computer before it has been uploaded. The UI reports publication only after verifying the remote.
Entries.Practice: Use Create a separate practice folder, initialize it deliberately, edit practice.txt, stage only that file, and inspect the local history. Use a local bare remote for upload practice.

Entries.Title: Choose what belongs in Git
Entries.Purpose: Ignore rules keep matching untracked files out of normal additions. They do not remove files already tracked or earlier copies of a secret.
Entries.Prerequisites: Review existing ignore files, project type, untracked files, and already tracked files.
Entries.Effects: Applying a rule edits an ignore file. The ignore file itself may be committed. Index removal is a separate action that should preserve the working file.
Entries.WhenToPause: Pause on likely credentials, private keys, environment files, or large binary assets. An ignore rule cannot repair a secret already published.
Entries.Outcome: The output identifies a matching rule when the path is ignored. A tracked file remains tracked.
Entries.Practice: Create build/output.txt in the practice repository; preview an ignore rule and check the affected list before applying it.

Entries.Title: A pull request is a review proposal
Entries.Purpose: A pull request describes a proposed merge from a published source branch into an explicitly selected target branch. Git pull downloads and integrates history; it is a different action.
Entries.Prerequisites: Published source commits, GitHub API sign-in, allowed repository permissions, and known source and target.
Entries.Effects: Creating a PR writes hosted collaboration metadata. It does not merge the branches or upload uncommitted files.
Entries.WhenToPause: Pause if the source is unpublished, the target or fork repository is uncertain, or a previous submission has an unknown outcome. Look for an existing matching request before retrying.
Entries.Outcome: A draft or ready request appears for review. Mergeability may remain pending; unknown does not mean conflict.
Entries.Practice: Read this lesson offline. Only create a real PR in a separately designated authorized sandbox.

Entries.Title: Understand and finish a merge conflict
Entries.Purpose: A conflict means Git needs your decision about overlapping or incompatible changes. Local and incoming versions are evidence, not an automatic right answer.
Entries.Prerequisites: A recorded merge operation, the conflicting file list, preserved pre-merge work, and an editor.
Entries.Effects: Edit the intended combined content, inspect the result, stage resolved paths, and continue the supported merge. Abort attempts operation-specific recovery.
Entries.WhenToPause: Pause for binary, rename/delete, or complex conflicts requiring developer review. Choosing one side for every file can lose intended work. Abort is not a universal backup.
Entries.Example:
git status
git diff --no-ext-diff --no-textconv
# Resolve a practice text file in an editor, then review:
git add -- practice.txt
git commit
Entries.Outcome: The recorded operation ends only after all conflicts are resolved and the merge commit or verified abort completes.
Entries.Practice: Use two disposable clones and a local bare remote to make competing changes to one text line. Inspect both histories before merging.

Entries.Title: Remote, upstream, and push destination
Entries.Purpose: A remote is a named connection to another repository. The upstream supplies the usual comparison and update target. The configured upload destination can be different, especially with forks.
Entries.Prerequisites: A known authorized repository URL and explicit current branch.
Entries.Effects: Reading these relationships changes nothing. Configuring a remote or tracking branch changes local Git configuration and needs review.
Entries.WhenToPause: Pause if multiple upload mappings exist, tracking is missing, or the remote contains unrelated history. Never assume origin/main for every project.
Entries.Outcome: Remote addresses and branch tracking are visible. Unknown tracking is shown as unknown rather than zero incoming commits.
Entries.Practice: Use separate local bare repositories in practice and compare a configured upstream with a different push remote.
